# Desargues Involution Theorem and Isoconjugations

## Desargues Involution Theorem

:::{#thm-desarguesInvolutionTheorem}
## Desargues involution theorem, DIT
Let $A,B,C,D$ be four points on the conic $\mathcal{C}$, and let $\ell$ be a line not passing through $A,B,C,D$. Suppose that $\ell$ intersects $\mathcal{C}$ at points $X,Y$, then
$$
(X,Y),\,(AB\cap \ell,CD\cap \ell),\, (AC\cap\ell,BD\cap \ell),\, (AD\cap\ell, BC\cap\ell)
$$
is an involution.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Note that
$$
(X,Y;\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap AC)\stackrel{A}{=}(X,Y;B,C)_{\mathcal{C}}\stackrel{D}{=}(X,Y;\ell\cap DB,\ell\cap DC)=(Y,X;\ell\cap DC,\ell\cap DB)
$$
This shows that $(X,Y),(\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap CD),(\ell\cap AC,\ell\cap BD)$ is an involution. The same argument applies for the fourth pair.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
From DIT, given points $A,B,C,D$ (no three of which are collinear) and a line $\ell$ not passing through $A,B,C,D$, the map
$$
g:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to\mathbb{P}_\ell,\,X\mapsto\ell\cap (ABCDX)
$$
(where $\ell\cap (ABCDX)$ denotes the second intersection of $\ell$ and $(ABCDX)$) is an involution. From this viewpoint, it is natural to regard $\mathbb{P}_{AB}\cup\mathbb{P}_{CD}$ as a conic.
:::

:::{#cor-tangentConicsDit}
Given points $A,B,C,D$ (no three of which are collinear) and a line $\ell$ not passing through any of them, there are exactly two conics passing through $A,B,C,D$ and tangent to $\ell$ (the tangency points are the fixed points of the involution).
:::

:::{#thm-ddit}
## DDIT
Let $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4\in\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}$ be tangent to a conic $\mathcal{C}$. Set $\ell_i\cap \ell_j=A_{ij}$ for $1\leq i<j\leq 4$. Suppose that $P$ is not on $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4$, and $m,n$ are the two tangents to $\mathcal{C}$ passing through $P$, then 
$$
(m,n),(PA_{12},PA_{34}),(PA_{13},PA_{24}),(PA_{14},PA_{23})
$$
is an involution.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This is the dual of Desargues involution theorem.
:::

In Desargues involution theorem, the points $A,B,C,D$ need not be distinct, and a line becomes a tangent when they coincide. Dually, in DDIT, if two lines coincide, their intersection becomes the tangency point.

:::{#thm-carnot}
## Carnot theorem
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $A_1,A_2\in BC,\,B_1,B_2\in CA,\,C_1,C_2\in AB$. Fix point $P$ not on the three sides, then there exists a conic $\mathcal{C}$ intersecting the three sides of $ABC$ at $A_1,A_2,B_1,B_2,C_1,C_2$ if and only if
$$
\prod_{i=1}^2 A(B,C;P,A_i)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^2 B(C,A;P,B_i)\cdot  \prod_{i=1}^2 C(A,B;P,C_i)=1
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that such a conic $\mathcal{C}$ exists, then we apply DIT to the quadrangle $B_1C_1B_2C_2\in\mathcal{C}$ and line $BC$,
$$
(A_1,A_2),(B,C),(B_1C_1\cap BC,B_2C_2\cap BC)
$$
is an involution, i.e.
$$
(B,C;B_1C_1\cap BC,A_1)\cdot (B,C;B_2C_2\cap BC,A_2)=1
$$
However, $(B,C;B_iC_i\cap BC,A_i)=A(B,C;P,A_i)\cdot A(B,C;P,B_iC_i\cap BC)^{-1}$, from Menelaus theorem,
$$
(B,C;B_iC_i\cap BC,A_i)=-A(B,C;P,A_i)\cdot B(C,A;P,B_i)\cdot C(A,B;P,C_i)
$$
for $i=1,2$. Multiplying these for $i=1,2$ yields Carnot theorem.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
The equality in Carnot theorem is equivalent to the existence of an isoconjugation $\varphi$ on $ABC$ such that
$$
\varphi(AA_1)=AA_2,\,\varphi(BB_1)=BB_2,\,\varphi(CC_1)=CC_2
$$
We may take $\varphi$ to be the $(BB_1\cap CC_1,BB_2\cap CC_2)$-isoconjugation.
:::

From Carnot theorem and Ceva theorem, the vertices of two cevian triangles are conconic.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Let $P_aP_bP_c$ and $Q_aQ_bQ_c$ be the cevian triangles of points $P$ and $Q$ with respect to $ABC$, then the points
$$
P_a,\,P_b,\,P_c,\,Q_a,\,Q_b,\,Q_c
$$
are conconic. This conic is called the **Carnot conic** (or **Cevian conic**) of $P$ and $Q$. The Carnot conic of $P$ and $P$ (which is tangent to the three sides of $ABC$ at the vertices of the cevian triangle of $P$) is called the **inconic** of $P$ (with respect to $ABC$). The $P$-anticomplement of the inconic of $P$ is called the **circumconic** of $P$ (i.e. the conic tangent to the three sides of the anticevian triangle at $A,B,C$).
:::

## Isoconjugations and Circumconics


In @thm-isoconjugate, we defined the $(P,Q)$-isoconjugation $\varphi$, denoted $\varphi=P\times Q$.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. All points on side $BC$ (except for $B,C$) are sent to $A$ by $\varphi$, and $\varphi(A)$ is the entire line $BC$. This suggests that we should not consider the image of the vertices $A,B,C$ under isoconjugations when there is no additional structure (for instance, some lines or conics passing through the vertices).
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. A line $\ell$ passing through $A$ is sent to a line $\varphi(\ell)$ passing through $A$ by $\varphi$ (omitting the image of $A$ itself). We use the convention that $A\in \ell$ is sent to $\varphi(\ell)\cap BC\in \varphi(\ell)$ by $\varphi$. On the other hand, if a conic $\mathcal{C}$ passes through $A$, let $\ell$ be the tangent of $A$ to $\mathcal{C}$, and we use the convention that $A\in \mathcal{C}$ is sent to $\varphi(\ell)\cap BC\in\varphi(\mathcal{C})$ by $\varphi$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. Suppose that the tripolar of $P$ and $\varphi(P)$ are $\ell$ and $m$, respectively, then $\varphi(AP)=A\varphi(P)$. From harmonicity, $\varphi(A(\ell\cap BC))=A(m\cap BC)$.
:::

:::{#lem-isoconjline}
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. Suppose that the tripolar of point $P$ is $\ell$, the circumconic of $\varphi(P)$ is $\mathcal{C}$, then 
$$\varphi(\ell)=\mathcal{C},\,\varphi(\mathcal{C})=\ell$$
and $\varphi:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to \mathcal{C}$ is a projective map.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that $X$ is on $\ell$, then
$$
f:\mathbb{L}_B\to \mathbb{L}_C,\,B\varphi(X)\mapsto BX\mapsto X\mapsto CX\mapsto C\varphi(X)
$$
is projective. By Steiner conic, the locus of $\varphi(X)=B\varphi(X)\cap C\varphi(X)$ is a conic $\mathcal{C}'$ through $B,C$. Similarly, $\mathcal{C}'$ is a circumconic (i.e. a conic passing through the three vertices). Let the tripolar of $\varphi(P)$ be $m$, then the tangent of $C$ to $\mathcal{C}'$ is
$$
f(BC)=\varphi(C(\ell\cap AB))=C(m\cap AB)
$$
Note that this is the tangent of $C$ to $\mathcal{C}$, so we similarly see that $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}'=\varphi(\ell)$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Let $\varphi=P\times P$. Suppose that $\ell$ is the tripolar of $P$, then $\varphi(\ell)$ is the circumconic of $P$.
:::

We may similarly prove the following example by Steiner conic.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
A conic $\mathcal{C}$ passing through $B$, $C$ (but not through $A$) is sent to a conic through $B,C$ by an isoconjugation.
:::

:::{#lem-trilineardual}
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$, and let $P,Q$ be points not on the sides of $ABC$. The following statements are equivalent.

(1) $P$ is on the circumconic of $Q$.

(2) $Q$ is on the tripolar of $P$.

(3) $\varphi(Q)$ is on the circumconic of $\varphi(P)$.

(4) $\varphi(P)$ is on the tripolar of $\varphi(Q)$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that $P$ is on the circumconic of $Q$. Let $P_aP_bP_c$ and $Q_aQ_bQ_c$ be the cevian triangles of $P$ and $Q$, respectively, then the tripolar of $P$ passes through the harmonic conjugate $P_b'$ of $P_b$ with respect to $A|C$ and the harmonic conjugate $P_c'$ of $P_c$ with respect to $A|B$. Consider the projective map
$$
f:\mathbb{L}_{AC}\to \mathbb{L}_{AB},\,P_b'\mapsto P_b\mapsto P\mapsto P_c\mapsto P_c'
$$
Since $f(A)=A,\,f(C)=Q_c,\,f(B)=Q_b$, the tripolar $P_b'P_c'$ of $P$ passes through a fixed point $Q$ as $P$ varies.

This shows that (1)$\implies$(2) and (3)$\implies$(4). From @lem-isoconjline, (2)$\implies$(3) and (4)$\implies$(1).
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
Given an isoconjugation $\varphi$ on $ABC$, $P$ is on the tripolar of $\varphi(Q)$ if and only if $Q$ is on the tripolar of $\varphi(P)$. This may be regarded as the tripolar version of La Hire theorem. Define $\mathfrak{p}(X)$ to be the tripolar of $\varphi(X)$, then $\mathfrak{p}$ is a dual transformation such that $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is the identity, so $\mathfrak{p}$ is indeed a polar transformation by @polarequiv.
:::

:::{#lem-isoquadrilateral}
Let $\varphi=X\times X'=Y\times Y'$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$, then 
$$
\varphi(XY\cap X'Y')= XY'\cap X'Y
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $XY\cap X'Y'=Z$, $XY'\cap X'Y=Z'$. Apply DDIT to the quadrilateral formed by lines $XY,X'Y',XY',X'Y$ and point $A$,
$$
(AX,AX'),(AY,AY'),(AZ,AZ')
$$
is an involution. A similar argument on the vertices $B$ and $C$ shows that $\varphi(Z)=Z'$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
In @lem-isoquadrilateral, if $A,X,Y$ are collinear, then $X\varphi(Y)\cap Y\varphi(X)$ is on $BC$.
:::

:::{#lem-isoconconic}
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. Suppose that $P,Q$ are points such that line $PQ$ does not pass through $A,B,C$, then 
$$
A,\,B,\,C,\,P,\,Q,\,P\varphi(Q)\cap Q\varphi(P)
$$
are conconic.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Note that $\varphi(P),\,\varphi(Q),\,PQ\cap\varphi(P)\varphi(Q)$ are collinear. From @lem-isoconjline and @lem-isoquadrilateral, $A,\,B,\,C,\,P,\,Q,\,P\varphi(Q)\cap Q\varphi(P)$ are conconic by applying $\varphi$.
:::

:::{#lem-fixed-points-isoconjugation}
Suppose that $\varphi=P\times P$ is an isoconjugation on $ABC$, then $\varphi(X)=X$ if and only if $X$ is equal to $P$ or one of the vertices of the anticevian triangle of $P$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Since $\varphi$ maps $AX$ to $AX$,
$$
A(B,C;P,X)=A(C,B;P,X)=A(B,C;X,P)
$$
We see that $A,X,P$ are collinear or $A(B,C;P,X)=-1$. Similarly, $X$ is equal to $P$ or one of the vertices of the anticevian triangle of $P$.
:::

The following lemma is a special case of @lem-isoconconic.

:::{#lem-tangent-conic-isoconjugation}
Suppose that $\varphi=P\times P$ is an isoconjugation on $ABC$, then line $P\varphi(X)$ is tangent to $(ABCPX)$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $P\varphi(X)$ intersect $(ABCPX)$ again at $Y$. Applying $\varphi$, $P\varphi(X)$ is sent to $(ABCPX)$, so $\varphi(Y)=Y$. From @lem-fixed-points-isoconjugation, $Y$ is equal to $P$ or one of the vertices of the anticevian triangle of $P$, but the latter are not on $(ABCPX)$, so $Y=P$.
:::

## The Fixed Points of an Isoconjugation and Desargues Involution Theorem

:::{#lem-isoconjugatefix}
An isoconjugation $\varphi$ on $ABC$ has exactly $4$ fixed points, that is, there are four points $P$ satisfying $\varphi(P)=P$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Since $BX\mapsto B\varphi(X)$ is an involution, there are two fixed lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$. Similarly argument on the vertex $C$ gives two fixed lines $m_1,m_2$, then the fixed points are precisely the four intersections $\ell_i\cap m_j$, $i,j=1,2$.
:::

This shows that isoconjugation is uniquely determined by the four fixed points: the cevian triangle of the four fixed poins is the triangle where the isoconjugation is defined on.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Let $P,Q,R,S$ be four points (no three of which are collinear) such that the cevian triangle of $PQRS$ is $ABC$. Define the isoconjugation of the complete quadrangle $PQRS$ to be the isoconjugation $\varphi$ on $ABC$ such that $\varphi(P)=P$.
:::

:::{#thm-quadrangle-isoconjugation}
Let $\varphi$ be the isoconjugation of the complete quadrangle $PQRS$. For any conic $\mathcal{C}$ passing through $P,Q,R,S$, $X$ and $\varphi(X)$ are conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\ell=X\varphi(X)$, and let $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}$ intersect at points $U,V$. We apply DIT to the quadrangle $PQRS$ on $\mathcal{C}$ and the line $\ell$,
$$
(U,V),(\ell\cap PQ,\ell\cap RS), (\ell\cap PR,\ell\cap QS),(\ell\cap PS,\ell\cap QR)
$$
is an involution. Let $ABC$ be the cevian triangle of $P$ with respect to $QRS$, then from the definition of isoconjugation,
$$
-1=A(X,\varphi(X);P,R)=(X,\varphi(X);PQ\cap \ell,RS\cap\ell)
$$
This shows that the harmonic conjugation with respect to $X|\varphi(X)$ sends $PQ\cap \ell$ to $RS\cap\ell$, and similarly, we see that the involution we obtained from DIT is the harmonic conjugation with respect to $X|\varphi(X)$, i.e. $(X,\varphi(X);U,V)=-1$. We conclude that $X$ and $\varphi(X)$ are conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

:::{#lem-eight-point-conic}
Suppose that the anticevian triangles of points $P,Q$ are $P_AP_BP_C$ and $Q_AQ_BQ_C$, respectively, then
$$
P,\,P_A,\,P_B,\,P_C,\,Q,\,Q_A,\,Q_B,\,Q_C
$$
are conconic. We call this conic the **eight-point conic** of $P,Q$ (with respect to $ABC$).
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\mathcal{G}=(PP_AP_BP_CQ)$. Triangle $ABC$ is self-conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{G}$, so $A,AQ\cap BC$ are conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{G}$. Note that
$$
(A,AQ\cap BC;Q,Q_A)=-1
$$
Since $Q$ is on $\mathcal{G}$, $Q_A$ is also on $\mathcal{G}$ by La Hire theorem. Similarly the eight points are conconic on $\mathcal{G}$.
:::

In other words, if two complete quadrangles share the same cevian triangles, then the eight vertices are conconic. Sometimes, the eight-point conic may degenerate into two lines.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
稱三個$ABC$上等共軛$\varphi_i$，$i=1,2,3$共線若對於所有$X$，$\varphi_i(X)$共線。
:::

:::{#lem-isoconjugateline}
$\varphi_i$共線若且唯若存在一點$X$使$X_i:=\varphi_i(X)$共線。
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
取$\varphi_1,\varphi_2$的不動點的八點錐線$\mathcal{G}$，由等共軛性質，$X$對$\mathcal{G}$極線就是$X_1X_2$。因為$X_3\in X_1X_2$，所以$\varphi_3$不動點也在$\mathcal{G}$上。給定$Y$，由等共軛知$Y_1,\,Y_2,\,Y_3$共線。
:::

@lem-isoconjugateline 也可以直接證明：給定$Y$，$(X\div Y)\times X_i=Y_i$，而$X\div Y$是射影變換。

:::{#cor-diagonalconic}
把跟兩個等共軛$\varphi_1,\varphi_2$共線的所有等共軛$\varphi$蒐集起來，這些$\varphi$的不動點形成一個錐線$\mathcal{G}$，並且對於所有$X\in \mathbb{P}$，$\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}(X)= \varphi_1(X)\varphi_2(X)$。
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
給定點$P$與線$\ell$，則$P\times X$共線對於$X\in \ell$，將這些等共軛蒐集起來記為$P\times \ell$。由@cor-diagonalconic ，$P\times \ell$可以視為配極(滿足$P$的極線是$\ell$且$ABC$自共軛)。
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
@lem-trilineardual 中(下面的Remark)，給定等共軛$\varphi=P\times Q$，則存在錐線$\mathcal{G}$使得$\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}(X)$的三線性極點就是$\varphi(X)$。令$Q$的三線性極線為$\ell$，則$\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}(P)=\ell$，這說明了$P\times \ell=\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}$，也就是說定義$P\times Q$的錐線與定義$P\times \ell$的錐線都是$\mathcal{G}$。
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
考慮等共軛的對偶命題：給定三角形$ABC$與直線$\ell_1,\ell_2$，令$f_A$為對合相互對$(B,C),\,(\ell_1\cap BC,\ell_2\cap BC)$定義的對合，對稱地定義$f_B,f_C$，則定義線等共軛$\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}=\ell_1\times \ell_2$滿足對於直線$m$，直線$\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}(m)$通過$f_A(m\cap BC),\,f_B(m\cap CA),\,f_C(m\cap AB)$。
:::

令$\ell_1,\ell_2,m$的三線性極點為$P_1,P_2,Q$，並定義$\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}=\ell_1\times \ell_2$，$\varphi=P_1\times P_2$，則$\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}(m)$的三線性極點為$\varphi(Q)$。這說明了線等共軛變換與等共軛變換之間透過三線性極線有對應關係。注意到定義$\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}$與$\varphi$的錐線都是$\mathcal{G}$，其中$\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}=P_1\times \ell_2=P_2\times \ell_1$。

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
@thm-isoconjugate 中定義的等共軛變換應該稱為點等共軛變換，用$\varphi^\mathbb{P}$記，但因為習慣以點的角度出發，故會省略而稱之為等共軛變換。
:::
